newsitem.title: UK: Credit surge ups pressure for higher British rates.
newsitem.headline: Credit surge ups pressure for higher British rates.

text.p: British personal borrowing soared by more than one billion pounds ($1.6 billion) in February, official figures showed on Wednesday.
Analysts said this boosted the chances of a post-election interest rate rise to keep consumers in check.
The Bank of England said net consumer credit leapt by 1.22 billion pounds in February, the largest rise on record, compared with 844 million pounds in January and 652 million in February last year.

The surge in personal borrowing means the next Chancellor of the Exchequer, of whichever party, will be under intense pressure to raise interest rates within weeks of taking office after the May 1 election, and maybe by half a point rather than just a quarter, financial analysts said.

"Consumer borrowing continues to grow at quite a healthy pace," said CIBC chief economist David Coleman. "It keeps the pressure on whoever is the next Chancellor to raise rates just as the U.S. has done."
Analysts said the strong consumer credit was somewhat offset by the softer than expected growth in narrow money supply, a measure of notes and coins in circulation.
UK MO grew 6.4 percent year on year in March, less than the 6.5 percent forecast, despite a possible boost from the Easter weekend, which fell seven days earlier than last year.
However, this rate of growth is still well above the upper limit of the government's monitoring range of 4.0 percent and suggests inflationary pressures may be building.
Underlying inflation is expected to fall in the next few months. It edged down to 2.9 percent in February from 3.1 percent in January.
But evidence of robust economic activity -- especially in the consumer sector -- is fuelling expectations that a rate rise will take place to keep it in check.
"There's no sign of inflation yet but then there's no sign of inflation yet in the United States and rates are going up there," said Coleman.
The U.S. central bank raised official interest rates by a quarter point to 5.5 percent last week.

If opinion polls are right and the Conservative government is ousted by the Labour Party in the election, Chancellor Kenneth Clarke is likely to be replaced by Gordon Brown, the shadow finance minister.
Coleman said he could gain valuable credibility by raising rates by a half point.

"With a new government there is an argument for a 50 point rise straight away -- getting the financial markets on your side with a tough policy and one that doesn't cost you anything in the first year of government." ($ = 0.606 British Pounds)
